import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 938

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/938](https://www.erdosproblems.com/938)
-/
open Nat

namespace Erdos938

/--
Let $A=\{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots\}$ be the sequence of powerful numbers (if $p\mid n$ then $p^2\mid n$).
Are there only finitely many three-term progressions of consecutive terms $n_k,n_{k+1},n_{k+2}$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_938 : answer(sorry) ↔ {P : Finset ℕ | (P : Set ℕ).IsAPOfLength 3 ∧ ∃ k,
    P = {nth Powerful k, nth Powerful (k + 1), nth Powerful (k + 2)}}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos938

reformulations.difference: The Lean formulation counts a family of unordered Finsets obtained from Nat.nth Nat.Powerful, rather than indices of the positive powerful-number sequence. Nat.Powerful also admits zero, and k ranges over all naturals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Powerful numbers contain every square, so they are infinite and Nat.nth is their strictly increasing enumeration, without default-value cases. Its first terms are 0, 1, 4; restricting to indices k ≥ 1 gives exactly the positive powerful-number sequence. For a < b < c, the set {a,b,c} satisfies IsAPOfLength 3 exactly when a+c=2*b. The map sending k to its three consecutive terms as a Finset is injective, since its least element determines k. Thus finiteness of the Finset family is equivalent to finiteness of the qualifying indices. The only extra index, k=0, produces {0,1,4}, which is not an AP. Review938.main_equivalence in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves the displayed finiteness proposition equivalent to finiteness of {k : ℕ | 0 < k ∧ nth Powerful k + nth Powerful (k+2) = 2 * nth Powerful (k+1)}. The enumeration and AP characterizations are also proved there; these proofs do not depend on the conjecture's sorry.
